However, if one of these vestot comes at a known time, such as if she yawned on this Rosh Chodesh and saw blood, and likewise until three Rosh Chodesh occurrences or four times at an interval of twenty to twenty or more, she establishes for herself a vest for the time and the physical symptom together. This means that on every such day when she has this symptom, she must be concerned and shall not have relations. But if the time arrived and the symptom did not come, or if the symptom came and the time did not arrive, she is not concerned.

Our teacher, the Rema, wrote in section 19 that this is specifically when she established a veset for both of them together, but initially she is concerned for each one individually because she does not know which of them she will establish; and as has been explained above regarding a veset of skipping and days, or from an interval and with days. Thus far his words. And it is simple, for a veset of a bodily occurrence is like a veset of days according to most poskim. And when she established it for both of them together, some say that then, when the time arrived and both did not come together, she is not concerned at all even as a veset that is not established, neither for the veset of the occurrence nor for the veset of the day [Shach, subsection 56]. And some say that she is certainly concerned for the day as a veset that is not established [Chavat Daat, subsection 26], for so ruled our teacher, the Beit Yosef, in section 25. This is his wording: If one of these comes at a known time, then she is certainly forbidden the entire onah of the veset, just as for a veset of days alone. Thus far his words. And according to this, it must be said that that which the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote, that in a case where she established it for both of them together, if the time arrived and the sensation did not come etc. she is not concerned, thus far his words, this means that she is not concerned as an established veset, such that if the time passed and she did not examine herself she is permitted, and so the Rosh wrote explicitly; but to be concerned for this onah as a veset that is not established, she is certainly concerned [and so wrote the Beit Yosef and the Bach]. For so the Rashba explained in Torat HaBayit, that for a veset of yawning alone she is not concerned until the yawning begins, but when it is composed of both of them, she is forbidden that entire onah even though the yawning has not yet begun; see there [and the words of the Shach are truly astonishing, and he himself wrote almost explicitly so in subsection 61; see there and examine closely].

If she yawned two times on Rosh Chodesh and saw, and afterwards she yawned not on Rosh Chodesh and saw, the matter is clarified that Rosh Chodesh does not cause the veset, but rather the yawning, and she has established a veset for yawning alone. And similarly, if on the third time she saw on Rosh Chodesh without yawning, the matter is clarified that the yawning is not the cause, but rather the Rosh Chodesh, and she has established a veset for Rosh Chodesh alone. But if she yawned two times on Rosh Chodesh, and on the third time she yawned on the twenty-ninth of the month and did not see, and on Rosh Chodesh she saw without yawning, she has established for herself a veset for the yawning of Rosh Chodesh, and we say that the yawning of yesterday caused the seeing of Rosh Chodesh. And in this everyone agrees, and it is not similar to the jumpings of section 51 for the reason we explained there. And know that this which we wrote, that she yawned on the twenty-ninth and saw on Rosh Chodesh, this is when Rosh Chodesh is one day, or when it is two days and she saw on the first day of Rosh Chodesh and not on the second day of Rosh Chodesh, for it is only effective for the previous day, as I wrote in section 52 regarding jumpings, and the same law applies to yawning.

If she yawned on Rosh Chodesh and saw, and then yawned again during the days of the month, she must be concerned for that yawning and is forbidden from engaging in relations until she examines herself. For every veset, whether of days or of the body, one must be concerned for it after one occurrence, and there is a concern lest she establish a veset for yawning without a known time. And if she examined herself and found that she did not see, she is no longer concerned for the yawning alone, but she is concerned for Rosh Chodesh lest she establish it for Rosh Chodesh; for even without this, it is the veset habeinoni for which every woman must be concerned before she has established for herself a fixed veset. But for the yawning, there is no need to be concerned, as it was uprooted in one instance according to the law of a veset that is not fixed [see Shach, subsection 60].

And know that this wording that we wrote, that if she yawned again during the days of the month she is concerned and is forbidden to have relations until she examines herself, so wrote the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch in section 21. And they raised a difficulty regarding this, for we hold that regarding a veset that is not established, if the veset passed and she did not examine herself, she is permitted without an examination. Therefore they wrote that a veset of yawning is more stringent, for since it is the nature of a woman to yawn at the time of her seeing or close to it, it is like a visible flaw before us, and she is forbidden even afterwards until she examines herself [Taz subsection 38 and Chavat Da'at]. And the matter is wondrous, to be more stringent regarding a veset of the body than a veset of the days, for they explicitly wrote in section 26 that they have one law; see there. And from all the Rishonim it does not appear so. And it seems more likely like the one who explains that it means ab initio, that ab initio she is forbidden to have relations until she examines herself [Prisha sign 65]. And furthermore, it is possible to say that regarding a veset of the days, where the concern is the entire onah, the matter is clearly recognizable that when the onah has passed she is permitted; but regarding a veset of the body, where the concern is only for their time, as will be explained with the help of Heaven, and when the hour that she was accustomed to yawn has passed she is permitted. And if so, here too, when she yawned again she is concerned, for this is the explanation: when she yawned again, at this hour she is concerned, and when the hour has passed she is permitted. And this is certain, that it is impossible to be exact, and how could we permit her without an examination, for during the time of hours error is common, but not so regarding a veset of the day, for between day and night people do not err, as it is stated in the first chapter of Pesachim. And therefore the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch correctly say that she is forbidden until she examines herself, meaning if she desires to have relations after this hour; but if she waits several hours, she is permitted without an examination. And in practice, it requires further study, since the Acharonim agreed to be stringent and wrote that this is her hargashah [so wrote the Sidrei Taharah subsection 27 and the Ma'ayan Ganim in chapter 9 in the Chiddushim sign 11].

And such is the law regarding days: if she yawned today and yawned at the end of twenty days, if she yawns even not on the twentieth day, she must be concerned for that yawning, lest she establish a veset for yawning alone. If she yawned within twenty days and did not see, she no longer needs to be concerned for yawning alone, but she must be concerned for the end of twenty days. And similarly, she must be concerned for the fixed day of the month on which she yawned, lest she establish a veset for days. And similarly, she must be concerned for the veset ha-beinoni, which is thirty days [In the Shulchan Aruch, section 22, "thirty" is written regarding this law, see there; and we wrote "twenty" intentionally so as not to err, for the concern of thirty is due to the veset ha-beinoni, and on another day one need not be concerned for this day, and examine this closely]:

All these vestot that are established by bodily occurrences that we have explained—one occurrence does not establish with another. That is to say, we do not combine to the three times a yawn with a sneeze; rather, whenever she yawned three times or sneezed three times and saw [blood], she has established a vest. But if she yawned one time and saw, and sneezed two times and saw, we do not combine them with one another, and so too anything similar to this. Thus the Rishonim agreed, and the reason is simple, for in one woman it is unlikely that all the occurrences would happen to her together; rather, this one has this occurrence and that one has that occurrence, and if so, how could we combine them with one another? And there is room to doubt if in the first time she had two occurrences, such as a yawn and a sneeze, and afterwards over a period of time she yawned alone or sneezed alone, if she must be concerned. And it appears that she does not need to be concerned when it was not exactly like the first time. Nevertheless, one must deliberate on this, for perhaps this occurrence was the primary one. See what I wrote in section 67.

One leniency regarding a veset of the body as opposed to a veset of days was taught by the sages in the Mishnah [63b], for regarding a veset of days it has already been explained that even if the veset is at the beginning of the day or at the end of the day, she must be concerned for the entire day. However, regarding vestot of the body, one is only concerned for their specific time, meaning the hour she is accustomed to this veset coming to her. How so? If she was accustomed to seeing blood at the time of the beginning of this veset, meaning at the beginning of the yawning, she is immediately forbidden for the entire duration of the yawning, for perhaps the primary one is the second or third yawn, and so too for the future until the yawning passes [see Chavat Da'at subsection 30]. But if she was accustomed to seeing at its end, she is only forbidden at its end, for since she has established a chazakah that she does not see blood until she yawns for an hour or two beforehand, she certainly will not see before then [ibid.]. And when the yawning has passed and she did not see, she is permitted even though she still stands within the onah, meaning within the day or within the night, for it is not similar in this to a veset of days, as I have written.

And regarding this law, the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 24: In what case are these things said? When the entire sighting is contained within the veset, but if the entire sighting is not contained within the veset, but rather continues also after the veset, she is forbidden from the beginning of the veset until the end of one onah. Thus far their words. And even though it was explained in siman 184 regarding a veset that continues for several days that we only follow the beginning of the veset, and even according to the one who is stringent there, he was only stringent to forbid according to the time of the veset that continues into the second onah, see there, this is specifically regarding two separate onot, for every onah—meaning day or night—is a time unto itself. But when the interior of the veset and after the veset are in one onah, since the sighting extended after the veset, the entire onah is seized by it [the Ra'avad in the book Ba'alei HaNefesh]. And there are further distinctions in this law from the law of siman 184 [see Beit Yosef and Shach subsection 62]. And it has already been explained that if one of these comes at a known time, she is forbidden for the entire onah like plain days [see Taz subsection 39 and Nekudat HaKesef, and their words are forced; and see Kereti U'Peleti and Minchat Yaakov that in truth the Ra'avad does not hold so, but in the Shulchan Aruch they did not bring his opinion, see there; and the words of the Shach subsection 61 have no understanding at all, as written by the Kereti U'Peleti and the Sidrei Taharah, and delve into this].

All the laws of bodily vesatot are like the vesatot of days; for just as she is concerned for a vesat of days after one occurrence, so too she is concerned for a bodily vesat after one occurrence. How so? If she yawned once and saw, when she yawns another time, she is concerned for it. And just as a vesat of days that is not established is uprooted by one occurrence—for even if she saw twice on a known day, if the third time arrived and she did not see, it is entirely uprooted—so it is with a bodily vesat. And just as a vesat of days established by three occurrences requires three uprootings and an examination, so it is with a bodily vesat established in the body. And from when is its uprooting? From when this incident occurs and she does not see. And if the incident of the bodily vesat was at a known time and was an established vesat, it is not uprooted unless this incident occurs three times at its time and she did not see. But by the incident alone without the time, or the time alone wherein she did not see, it is not uprooted. And this means that if three established days passed over her and she did not yawn and did not see, nevertheless, if she yawned afterward on that established day, she is concerned as long as she has not established another established vesat for herself. But as long as she did not yawn, it is certain that she is no longer concerned, since that day passed three times and she did not yawn and did not see [see Chavot Daat, subsection 42].

There is reason to doubt whether other occurrences are considered the uprooting of a veset; for example, if she had a fixed veset for yawning every Rosh Chodesh, and afterwards she saw on Rosh Chodesh by means of sneezing, and afterwards she saw by means of sneezing from below on Rosh Chodesh, and afterwards she saw on Rosh Chodesh by means of the lower abdomen, and similar cases. Do we say that since we do not join one occurrence to another regarding a fixed veset, as I wrote in section 61, it is automatically considered also an uprooting of the veset? Or perhaps regarding the uprooting of a veset it is not considered an uprooting, since these too are occurrences of the body? And it requires further study.

And likewise, there is one who is uncertain, according to what has been explained, that a bodily vest is like a vest of days, and a vest of jumping alone is not a vest except with days, as I wrote in section 46, if one combines a vest of jumping with a bodily vest as well—that is, she jumped and yawned and saw blood, and she did so three times, but when she jumped alone or yawned alone she did not see—whether we say that she established a vest for herself, such that whenever she jumps and yawns she is forbidden, just as with jumping on a known day. And even though in the Gemara [11a] jumping and days are explained, it cited one of them, and the same applies to jumping and yawning; or perhaps they do not combine and this is not a vest. Thus far his words.

And so too one should be in doubt regarding two things from the occurrences of the body, whether we are concerned for one [of them]; for example, if she yawned and sneezed three times and saw blood, whether she established a vest for herself specifically for yawning and sneezing, but for one of them she need not be concerned, or perhaps she is concerned even for one of them. And behold, this is certain: that if there occurred within the time before she established the vest a yawn alone or a sneeze alone and she did not see blood, she certainly did not establish [a vest] for one of them. And the doubt is if this did not occur within the time of establishing the vest, if afterwards one of them occurred, whether she should be concerned for this or not. And it appears that we require exactly according to the action that was at the time of the establishment and not in another manner, and so too regarding the previous doubt.

It has already been explained in section 43 that in the Gemara [63b] there is another type of veset through eating, such as if she ate garlic and saw, or ate peppers and saw. All the poskim did not mention this, and we exerted effort there to provide a reason for this, see there. However, our teacher, the Rema, mentioned this in section 23, and this is his wording: If she ate garlic and saw, ate onion and saw, or ate peppers and saw, some say she has established a veset for herself to see through any eating of hot things. And some say that whenever she sees through food, its law is like seeing through jumping or other actions she performs, which is called seeing through an accident, and she does not establish a veset except with the days. And some say its law is like a veset she sees through a physical occurrence in her body, and she establishes it even without equal days. Thus far his words.

And one should not ask according to the latter opinion that this is a vest of the body, if so, why regarding a vest of the body do we not combine one with another, such as a yawn with a sneeze, yet regarding eating we combine garlic, onion, and peppers? For they are not comparable; regarding occurrences, each occurrence is a matter unto itself, but regarding eating, where the proof is via the heating of the body from this eating, if so, what does it matter to me if it is garlic, or if it is onion or peppers, since they all heat the body? For it is for this reason that the first opinion holds that she has established a vest for all hot things, even if not from these three things. Nevertheless, it appears that even this is specifically when the establishment of the vest was via these three species, but if the establishment was via one of them, she has not established a vest for other foods, for perhaps this body is only affected by this species. However, when she established it via three species, she has established it for all species, just as in Bava Kamma, when [an ox] gored an ox, a donkey, and a camel, it becomes muad for all species [Bava Kamma 37b].

There is one who says that even though from these three types of foods she established a veset for all hot things, nevertheless, if she ate other hot things three times and did not see, the veset is not uprooted from these three types. However, if she ate one of these types three times and did not see, the veset is uprooted from all types [Chavat Da'at section 29]. There is also a proof for this from a mu'ad in Bava Kamma there [37b]. And there is a doubt if she ate garlic and saw, and ate another hot type and did not see, and ate onion and saw, and peppers and saw, whether the other type that she ate and did not see is an interruption and she did not establish a veset for these three things, or since the Gemara counted them, perhaps they have more heat than all other hot things in the world. And regarding one type in such a case, there is certainly no doubt, such as if she ate garlic three times and saw, even though in the meantime she ate onion and did not see, nevertheless she established a veset for garlic, for we see that her body is affected only by this type. The doubt is only if the establishment was by means of three types, whether another type interrupts between them, and it requires further study.

According to the law of the Gemara, a woman does not establish a vest during her days of niddah or her days of zivah, as will be explained. It is stated in the Gemara [11a] that specifically from an "open spring" she does not establish it during her days of niddah, but from a "closed spring" she does establish it; see there, for this refers only to her days of niddah, but during her days of zivah she does not establish it even from a closed spring. However, the Tur wrote, and this is his wording: According to the law of the Talmud, a woman does not establish a vest neither during the days of niddah nor during the days of zivah. How so? If she saw on the first of the month and on the fifth of it, which is within the days of niddah for the first seeing, even if she conducted herself so three times, she has not established a vest for the fifth of the month, but rather for the first of the month. And similarly, if she saw on the first of the month and on the fifteenth of it, she has not established a vest for the fifteenth, as it is within the days of zivah. In what case does this apply? When she saw the first seeing from an open spring, as I have explained. But if she saw it from a closed spring—for example, if she saw twice on Rosh Chodesh, and on the third time she saw on the twenty-fifth of the month and on Rosh Chodesh—even though the third seeing was within her days of niddah for the seeing of the twenty-fifth of the month, she establishes it on Rosh Chodesh, because the first two were from a closed spring, and the seeing of the twenty-fifth of the month was due to excess blood that increased within her and hurried to come; and she must also be concerned for the day of the earlier seeing, lest she is establishing a different vest. Thus far the words of the Tur. [And this fact that she does not establish it during the days of zivah at all is according to the words of Shmuel on 39a].

And this is according to the approach of Rashi and Tosafot and all our teachers regarding the laws of niddah and zavah; therefore, they were forced to struggle with the interpretation of "a closed fountain," that it refers to the first two sightings. However, according to the Rambam, who holds that a woman counts the days of niddah and the days of zavah all her days, whether she saw or did not see, as I wrote in siman 183, the interpretation is simple: it is called "an open fountain" when she actually saw, for then she does not establish a veset during her niddah days; and "a closed fountain" is when she did not actually see, but rather according to the calculation she stands within her niddah days, for then she establishes a veset. And so it is explained from his words in chapter 8, law 9, see there; and see what I wrote in siman 183.

All of this was in the time of the Gemara, but nowadays the Tur wrote in the name of the Ramban that since it is the custom not to distinguish between the days of niddah and the days of zivah—meaning that for every drop of blood they sit seven clean days according to the law of a zavah—the same applies regarding the establishment of a veset, there is no distinction. Therefore, if she saw from the fifteenth to the fifteenth day, she has established a veset for herself. Thus far his words. For this reason, our teachers, the authors of the Shulchan Aruch, omitted this entire law. However, I am astonished, for if so, this stringency will lead to a great leniency; for example, if she has a veset every twenty days and it is a fixed veset, and afterward she sees three times from the fifteenth to the fifteenth, she would uproot the first veset, yet this is not a veset at all according to the essential law of the Torah, so how can it uproot the first fixed veset? And perhaps you will say that in truth, in such a case the first is not uprooted; if so, our teachers should have explained this law in any event. It requires further study.

And regarding the law, I have indeed seen one who ruled accordingly, that for leniency we do not say even in this time that it shall be called a vest in the days of niddah and zivah [Shach, subsection 71]. And there is one who disagrees in this [Minchat Yaakov, and see Kereti U'Peleti, subsection 30] and gave a reason that if so, they must calculate the days of niddah and zivah, and behold, the entire essence of the stringency that the daughters of Israel took upon themselves was for the purpose of not calculating the days of niddah and zivah. And in my humble opinion, this is no comparison at all, for they only need to know that any vest that comes in less than nineteen days to nineteen days is not a vest for leniency.

It appears to me that this is indeed the opinion of the Ra'avad in the book Ba'al HaNefesh regarding the matter of establishing a vestet within a vestet, as the Tur and the Shulchan Aruch wrote in section 32. This is his wording: Sometimes a woman establishes for herself a vestet within a vestet. How so? She saw three times on Rosh Chodesh, and the fourth time on the twentieth [so it should be, as the Shach wrote in subsection 72] of the month and on Rosh Chodesh, and similarly on the fifth and sixth times; behold, she has established two vestetot. Thus far his words. Meaning, a vestet on every Rosh Chodesh and another vestet on every twentieth of the month. And it is difficult: why is it relevant to call this a vestet within a vestet? Let us say that this woman has a vestet of intervals, for she sees once at twenty days and once at ten days, since she established it in this manner three times, on the fourth, fifth, and sixth. Rather, it is certainly because in ten days it is impossible to establish a vestet, as they are within the days of zivah, and according to the essential law one would not need to be concerned for this; however, as a stringency we say that she establishes it even during the days of zivah, but the primary vestet is from thirty days to thirty days, and therefore they call it a vestet within a vestet. [And see the Shach, subsection 72, who brought the wording of the Ra'avad, and our words should be aligned with his intention; and the Taz, subsection 47, and the Derishah read "on the second of the month" and were very pressed, see there; and the main point is like the Shach, and examine it closely].

It has already been explained at the beginning of the siman that there are women who do not have a fixed veset like other women, and they are four women: a virgin who has not reached twelve years and one day, which is the time of her naarut, or she has reached her years but has not brought signs; and an elderly woman who has ceased from seeing; and a pregnant woman; and a nursing woman. And they are not similar to one another, for the majority of virgins and elderly women have no time of seeing at all, and nevertheless, if they establish a veset three times, they are like all other women, for regarding this one we see that the time of her seeing has arrived, and regarding this one we see that her blood has not departed. However, in certain details there is a difference between them and other women. But a pregnant woman and a nursing woman, who due to the fetus are in a state of presumption of the departure of blood and not because of their years, have no veset at all, as will be explained with the help of Heaven.

How is it with a betulah? And it is not specifically a betulah, but rather even a married woman, if she has not reached her years even if she brought signs, or if she reached her years and was examined and signs were not found in her, she does not have the status of one who sees and she has no veset she-eino kavua. That is to say, that regarding other women they are concerned even for a veset she-eino kavua, yet this one, even if she saw one time or two times, is not concerned at all, and we say it is a mere occurrence. However, when she saw three times on a specific day of the month, or four times in a veset of intervals, she has established for herself a veset like all women, for it has been revealed that she has entered the category of seeing; and so too with all types of vesetot.

Nevertheless, there is a difference between her and an adult woman, for with an adult woman, once she has established a veset through three occurrences, we require that she uproot it three times at the time of the veset she established. For example, if she established a veset for every two months, we require that three periods of two months pass for her without seeing blood. But this girl only requires that three average onot of thirty days pass for her without seeing blood, and she has uprooted the veset entirely and is not concerned at all for the previous veset and has returned to her former status, and we say that some happenstance occurred regarding her seeing blood. Furthermore, even if she returned to seeing blood afterward at those times she was accustomed to seeing previously, she is not concerned until she returns and establishes it three times, because she is not prone to blood, and it was revealed that the first three times were happenstance; therefore, even now her law is as if she only now began to see blood.

And some say that specifically in this case, but if her seeing was three times in short intervals and she ceased from seeing for three such short intervals as she had seen, if she afterwards saw in that interval even one time, she is concerned for her seeing or for a medium interval like other women; specifically when she ceased for ninety days, which is three medium intervals, for we have seen that the nature ceased from her like other women, then we say that the first sightings were accidents. But in short intervals, her law is like other women [Shach subsection 66 and Derisha]. But from the words of the Rashba in Torat HaBayit in the Gate of Vestot it does not appear so, for he wrote, and this is his wording: A minor who has not reached her time etc. and we conclude that the same applies if she saw in short intervals after three initial intervals passed over her, because she is removed from blood and returned to her former status as if she had not seen from the beginning, for now it is revealed that those first three sightings were an accident, and therefore until she returns again to see three sightings etc. and the first veset is as if it is not, and she is not concerned for it until she sees another three sightings. Thus far his words. And so it appears from the Tur and Shulchan Aruch section 31 regarding an old woman, who wrote: If she returned to see in short intervals that she was accustomed to etc. she returns to her first fixed status etc. even with one time she returns to her former status etc. and in this the law of the old woman is more stringent than the law of the minor etc. Thus far his words. And why did they not explain that in short intervals even with one she is concerned? And it requires investigation; and even though there is a distinction to be made, nevertheless they should have explained it.

That which we have said, that when she has ceased for three average onot she does not concern herself with the first veset at all, if after she ceased for this duration—meaning ninety days—she saw, and again after ninety days she saw once more, and a third time after ninety days she saw once more, it is revealed that the first skipping was not a cessation of blood but rather a change of veset to once every ninety days, and she has established for herself a veset of haflagah. And one should not ask that we maintain that for a veset of haflagah four times are required so that there will be three haflagot, for the truth is that here too there are four haflagot, as we count the first skipping when she ceased until the ninety days as the first time, since it is now revealed that such is her veset. And it is simple that this is specifically when all the sightings were aligned from ninety to ninety and the like, such that they did not decrease or increase this sighting from another; but if she decreased or increased in one of them such that the sightings were not aligned, they do not combine with one another until she sees four aligned sightings.

And she is called an elderly woman whenever she has reached the years of old age such that they call her "mother" to her face, or even if they do not call her so, but she is fit to be called "mother"—and in our language, a father's mother or a mother's mother—and if they were to call her so to her face she would not object and is not concerned by this at all. Such an elderly woman, for whom three average intervals passed since she grew old and she did not see, behold she is one whose blood has ceased, and she is not concerned for her previous vest. And even if she saw again during an average interval, her law is like the law of a young girl who has not reached her time to see, for until three times she is not concerned, as she does not need to be concerned for a vest that is not fixed, like young girls. But if she returned to see during short intervals as she was accustomed to seeing during them, she has returned to her original fixedness even with one time regarding other vests, and regarding a gap, two times, if the gap was like before when she was accustomed to seeing with such a gap; for it has been revealed that the initial cessation was not a cessation but an accident. And in this, the law of the elderly woman is more stringent than a young girl, for regarding a young girl, after she stopped for three average intervals, even if she saw afterwards during short intervals as she used to see before, she is not concerned when she did not see three times; but an elderly woman is concerned even with one time, for regarding her it was revealed that she has not ceased at all, which is not the case with a young girl whom we must establish through sightings [and for this reason I cast doubt on the words of the Shach and the Perishah in section 79, although I have no complete proof from the Rashba and the Tur and Shulchan Aruch, see there, and also from the Gemara there is no proof, and examine this closely].

And similarly, a pregnant woman from the time her fetus is recognizable, which is three months into her pregnancy, and a nursing woman for all twenty-four months after the birth of the child, do not establish a vest. A pregnant woman before three months establishes a vest, even if we know she is pregnant, because before the fetus is recognizable her head and limbs are not heavy upon her [Beit Yosef in the name of the Rashba] and she is not in the status of one whose blood is removed. This is not the case after the recognition of the fetus. And a nursing woman, even if the child died or she gave her son to a wet-nurse, nevertheless does not establish a vest for all twenty-four months. For this status of a nursing woman as one whose blood is removed is not due to the milk alone, but because her limbs are disjointed at the time of her giving birth and do not return to their place until twenty-four months, and consequently because of this she is in the status of one whose blood is removed and they do not establish a vest. And although it is the opinion of the Ramban that they do establish a vest, as the Tur wrote in his name, nevertheless all our teachers do not hold so [and his opinion was not brought in the Shulchan Aruch, as the Shach wrote in subsection 73].

There is a stringency regarding a pregnant woman and a nursing woman over a virgin and an elderly woman, and there is a stringency regarding a virgin and an elderly woman over a pregnant woman and a nursing woman. How so is the stringency regarding a pregnant woman and a nursing woman? For regarding a virgin and an elderly woman, we explained that they do not concern themselves with a veset that is not fixed, and therefore they do not concern themselves with one or two sightings. However, a pregnant woman and a nursing woman concern themselves with a sighting that she sees, in the same manner that one concerns herself with a veset that is not fixed. The reason is that a girl and an elderly woman have no blood at all by nature, but a pregnant woman and a nursing woman have blood by nature, but the fetus or the milk obstructs it. And even though there are those who disagree and hold that they do not concern themselves [see Beit Yosef], nevertheless, we hold that they do concern themselves:

And there is a stringency regarding a virgin and an elderly woman more than a pregnant woman and a nursing woman, for regarding a virgin and an elderly woman, when they have seen three times they establish a veset, but a pregnant woman and a nursing woman do not concern themselves with the first veset. And even if they had an established veset and it arrived during this time, she does not require a bedikah and is permitted to her husband. And even if they are flowing with blood and see during those seasons that they were accustomed to see in, they do not concern themselves afterward, and we say that it was a chance occurrence. And the reason is also simple: for a virgin and an elderly woman do not have blood by nature, and yet these have seen, and we say that this one's time has arrived and this one's time has not yet ceased. But a pregnant woman and a nursing woman who have blood, but the fetus obstructs them, and it is impossible in any other way at all for such is the formation of man, if so, it is necessary that there was some chance occurrence in their seeing, and how could they establish a veset?

The days of pregnancy and nursing have passed, she returns to be concerned for her previous vestan. How so? If she had a vestat hayamim, if her vestat was on Rosh Chodesh, she is concerned for the first Rosh Chodesh that she encounters, and so too anything similar to this, even if she has not yet seen at all. And it follows that when she had a vestat haflagah, it is impossible for her to be concerned until she sees one time, and then she is concerned for her haflagah in the manner she was accustomed to separate. And regarding a vestat of a fixed day like Rosh Chodesh and its like, even if she did not see on the first Rosh Chodesh, she is concerned for the second, and if even then she did not see, she is concerned for the third [Beit Yosef]. If three Rosh Chodesh periods passed and she did not see, she is no longer concerned. And there are those who say that she is not concerned at all for the first Rosh Chodesh until she sees one time on Rosh Chodesh as she was accustomed to see previously, and then it becomes for her like a vestat kavua even though she saw only one time [see Shach, subsection 75]. And it is simple that specifically when she had a vestat kavua before the pregnancy she is concerned for it, but if she had a vestat she-eino kavua, she is not concerned for it at all. And know that a nursing woman after twenty-four months, even though she is still nursing, she is like all other women and is not in the legal status of one whose blood is removed [Gemara 9a].
